raw_text:
Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) were introduced to solve a central paradox of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI): the permanent metallic stent is most useful during the early months after balloon injury, but remains indefinitely, potentially impairing vasomotion, adaptive remodeling, non-invasive imaging, future bypass grafting, and late healing. Early first-in-human ABSORB experience with a poly-L-lactic acid everolimus-eluting scaffold suggested feasibility, late strut integration, restoration of vasomotor responses, and acceptable outcomes in simple lesions [1–5]. These observations created the “vascular restoration” hypothesis: temporary radial support plus antiproliferative drug delivery, followed by scaffold resorption and recovery of more physiologic vessel behavior [6,7].

The subsequent randomized evidence, however, showed that translating this concept into routine PCI was difficult. In the small EVERBIO II all-comers trial, angiographic late lumen loss and early clinical outcomes were broadly similar between Absorb BVS and contemporary drug-eluting stents (DES) [8]. ABSORB II initially reported similar 1- and 2-year clinical outcomes [9,10], but the 3-year primary mechanistic endpoints were not met and scaffold thrombosis emerged as a concern [11]. Four-year follow-up reinforced an excess of myocardial infarction and definite/probable device thrombosis with BVS [12]. The pivotal ABSORB III trial met non-inferiority for target-lesion failure at 1 year in selected, non-complex lesions [13], and ABSORB China and ABSORB Japan similarly supported short-term angiographic and clinical comparability in controlled populations [14,15]. In contrast, the pragmatic AIDA trial, enrolling broader “routine PCI” patients, found similar target-vessel failure but substantially higher device thrombosis with BVS [16]. Three- and five-year ABSORB III data confirmed higher cumulative target-lesion failure, target-vessel myocardial infarction, and scaffold thrombosis, although excess hazard appeared to attenuate after the expected resorption period [17,18].

Mechanistic analyses identified several explanations for these results. First-generation Absorb had relatively thick struts, limited overexpansion capacity, lower acute radial strength than cobalt-chromium DES, and susceptibility to malapposition, underexpansion, fracture, and intraluminal scaffold dismantling during resorption. Clinical event analyses linked adverse outcomes to small-vessel treatment, incomplete lesion preparation, and inadequate high-pressure post-dilation; optimized “PSP” implantation—prepare the lesion, size appropriately, post-dilate—was associated with better outcomes but did not fully eliminate risk [19]. Dedicated thrombosis analyses found scaffold thrombosis to be multifactorial, including procedural underexpansion, malapposition, small vessel size, premature antiplatelet discontinuation, and late structural discontinuity [20].

Meta-analyses consolidated the signal. Compared with contemporary everolimus-eluting metallic stents, Absorb BVS increased target-lesion failure, myocardial infarction, and definite/probable thrombosis at 2 to 3 years [21,22]. Longer-term pooled analyses suggested a time-varying pattern: excess risk was concentrated before complete bioresorption, whereas event rates beyond 3 years were more similar [23]. The final pooled ABSORB clinical program, including nearly 6,000 randomized patients, therefore provides a nuanced interpretation: first-generation polymeric BVS failed to match best-in-class DES during the active scaffold phase, but the original late-benefit hypothesis remains biologically plausible if early hazards can be reduced [24].

Special settings have not rescued routine use. In acute myocardial infarction, the thrombus-rich milieu and need for rapid, reliable expansion are challenging; randomized ISAR-Absorb MI data did not establish a compelling advantage of BVS over DES [25]. Nevertheless, acute coronary syndromes remain conceptually attractive because softer lipid-rich lesions may be easier to prepare, provided meticulous sizing, imaging, and antiplatelet adherence are achieved.

The field has therefore shifted from first-generation Absorb toward thinner-strut, faster-healing, more deliverable, and mechanically stronger platforms. Magnesium-based scaffolds were explored early in PROGRESS-AMS but were limited by recoil and restenosis [26,27]. Second-generation sirolimus-eluting absorbable magnesium scaffolds, including DREAMS 2G/Magmaris, showed improved angiographic performance and low scaffold thrombosis rates in BIOSOLVE studies, although the evidence base remains largely single-arm and focused on selected lesions [28–30]. Other emerging polymeric, iron-based, and hybrid scaffolds aim to combine thin struts, radiopacity, predictable degradation, adequate radial strength, and DES-like deliverability.

At present, contemporary metallic DES remain the default PCI platform because they are thin-strut, highly deliverable, safe, and supported by extensive randomized evidence. BVS should be viewed as an instructive but not yet established strategy: its promise is greatest in younger patients, large simple vessels, and scenarios where restoration of vasomotion or avoidance of a permanent implant may matter, but its use requires careful lesion selection, intravascular imaging when feasible, rigorous PSP technique, and prolonged attention to antiplatelet therapy. The next generation of scaffolds must demonstrate not merely non-inferiority in angiographic surrogates, but DES-like early safety plus durable clinical benefit after resorption.
